title: Retrieval-augmented answers
description: Chunk a local doc set, embed it, rank chunks by cosine similarity with numpy, and answer with citations code can check.
outcome: You can build a small RAG pipeline against any OpenAI-compatible embeddings endpoint and reject answers whose citations were not retrieved.
environment: Python 3.12 (macOS: brew python@3.12; Windows: python.org installer + py launcher), requests 2.34.2, numpy 2.5.4 (validated locally with 2.5.3); fake_model_server.py (/v1/embeddings + /api/embed); optional: Ollama 0.40.12 + embeddinggemma (622 MB) + qwen2.5:1.5b; equivalents (pending-ci): sqlite-vec 0.1.9, PostgreSQL 18 + pgvector 0.8.7
overview: Find the passages that matter, put them in the prompt with ids, and accept the answer only if it cites what was retrieved.
prerequisites: Lesson 4: validating model output in code

glossary.meaning: Vector of numbers representing a text; similar texts point in similar directions.
A passage cut from a document, small enough that several fit one prompt.
Dot product of two unit-length vectors: 1 = same direction, 0 = unrelated.
The k highest-scoring chunks returned by the search.
Every citation in the answer points to a chunk that was actually retrieved.

concepts: Retrieval runs in code; the model only reads what code selected.
Normalise vectors once, then cosine = one matrix product.
Citations are checked against the retrieved ids, not trusted.
Search always returns something: weak hits need a threshold.
inRealSystems: Ollama, llama.cpp (llama-server --embedding) and vLLM (pooling models) all serve POST /v1/embeddings.
Vectors usually live next to the data: sqlite-vec in SQLite, pgvector in PostgreSQL (HNSW index with vector_cosine_ops).
Production pipelines add re-ranking, metadata filters and an index refresh job.
useWhen: When answers must come from your own changing documents and you need a source to show; not for whole-corpus statistics.

codeWalkthrough.title: vectors / np.linalg.norm(...).clip(min=1e-12)
codeWalkthrough.detail: Normalise once at index time; afterwards `vectors @ q` is cosine similarity for every chunk in one step.

codeWalkthrough.title: np.argsort(-scores)[:k]
codeWalkthrough.detail: Descending sort of the scores, keep k: brute-force exact search - fine for thousands of chunks.

codeWalkthrough.title: f"[{cid}] {text}" inside <context>
codeWalkthrough.detail: Each chunk carries an id the model can cite; the id ties the answer back to a file and position.

codeWalkthrough.title: grounded = bool(cited) and set(cited) <= retrieved
codeWalkthrough.detail: Code, not the model, decides whether the answer is supported: no citation or an unknown id -> not grounded.

title: Agents with several tools
description: Offer three tools, let the model pick, validate every argument against JSON Schema in code, and return errors to the model so it can retry.
outcome: You can register tools with JSON Schemas, reject invalid calls before they run, and keep the loop alive through bad arguments.
environment: Python 3.12 (macOS: brew python@3.12; Windows: python.org installer + py launcher), requests 2.34.2; schema_check.py (stdlib JSON Schema subset); fake_model_server.py; equivalent (pending-ci): jsonschema 4.26.0; optional: Ollama 0.40.12 + qwen2.5:1.5b
overview: The model chooses among tools by their descriptions; your code checks each call against a schema and turns every failure into a message the model can act on.

glossary.meaning: The model's choice of which declared tool to call, based on names and descriptions.
Standard vocabulary for describing JSON (type, enum, minimum, required...); MCP and chat-completions tools use it.
Schema rule that rejects fields the schema does not declare.
A failure reported as the tool's result text, so the model can correct itself.

concepts: The registry is the allow-list.
Validate arguments before running anything.
Every failure is returned as text, never raised.
Clear, distinct descriptions drive correct tool choice.
inRealSystems: Chat-completions servers (Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM) pass tools[].function.parameters through as JSON Schema.
MCP tool definitions carry the same JSON Schema as inputSchema (lesson 10).
Production code uses a full validator (python-jsonschema, ajv) or generates schemas from types (Pydantic).
useWhen: When the next step depends on the request and tools have distinct jobs; call functions directly when the sequence is fixed.

title: State and memory
description: Keep conversation state within a token budget by summarising old turns, and store explicit long-term memory in SQLite.
outcome: You can budget tokens before every call, summarise to fit, and give an agent save/recall tools backed by a database file.
environment: Python 3.12 (macOS: brew python@3.12; Windows: python.org installer + py launcher), requests 2.34.2; sqlite3 (Python stdlib; SQLite 3.44 in the sandbox); fake_model_server.py; optional: Ollama 0.40.12 + qwen2.5:1.5b
overview: The message list is short-term state you must keep under the context window; facts that must survive go into SQLite through explicit tools.

glossary.meaning: Maximum tokens the model reads per request (Ollama default 4096; OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH or num_ctx change it).
The share of the window you allow for the prompt, leaving room for the reply.
Replace the oldest turns with one model-written summary when the budget is exceeded.
Facts stored outside the conversation (here SQLite) and fetched with a tool.

concepts: Check the budget before every model call.
Summaries lose detail; keep recent turns verbatim.
Memory writes are explicit tool calls you can audit.
SQL uses placeholders, never string formatting.
inRealSystems: Ollama defaults to a 4096-token window; OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH (server) or num_ctx (API options) change it, and RAM grows with it.
llama.cpp sets the window with -c/--ctx-size; MemGPT-style systems page memory in and out through tools.
useWhen: Summaries for long chats where the gist is enough; explicit memory for facts the user asks you to keep.

code:
"""Conversation state, summarise-to-fit a token budget, and explicit long-term memory in SQLite."""
import json
import os
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

import requests

BASE_URL = os.environ.get("LOCAL_MODEL_URL") or os.environ.get("BASE_URL", "http://localhost:11434/v1")
MODEL = os.environ.get("LOCAL_MODEL") or os.environ.get("MODEL", "qwen2.5:1.5b")
TOOLS = [{"type": "function", "function": {"name": n, "description": d, "parameters": {
    "type": "object", "properties": {k: {"type": "string", "maxLength": 300}}, "required": [k],
    "additionalProperties": False}}} for n, d, k in [
    ("save_memory", "Store a fact the user explicitly asked you to remember.", "note"),
    ("recall_memory", "Look up stored facts by keyword.", "query")]]


class MemoryStore:
    """Long-term memory = rows in a SQLite file; survives restarts, unlike the message list."""
    def __init__(self, path=":memory:"):
        self.db = sqlite3.connect(path)
        self.db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, note TEXT NOT NULL)")

    def save(self, note):
        with self.db:  # commits on success
            return f"saved note {self.db.execute('INSERT INTO notes (note) VALUES (?)', (note,)).lastrowid}"

    def recall(self, query, limit=3):
        words = [w for w in query.lower().split() if len(w) > 2] or [query.lower()]
        where = " OR ".join("lower(note) LIKE ?" for _ in words)  # placeholders only: no SQL injection
        rows = self.db.execute(f"SELECT id, note FROM notes WHERE {where} ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT ?",
                               [f"%{w}%" for w in words] + [limit]).fetchall()
        return "; ".join(f"{i}: {n}" for i, n in rows) or "no matching notes"

    def close(self):
        self.db.close()


def count_tokens(messages):
    # budget estimate = words (the fake server counts words too); real tokenizers differ -> compare usage.prompt_tokens
    return sum(len((m.get("content") or "").split()) for m in messages)


class Chat:
    def __init__(self, memory, budget=60, keep_last=2, base_url=BASE_URL, model=MODEL):
        self.messages = [{"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant with a memory tool."}]
        self.memory, self.budget, self.keep_last = memory, budget, keep_last
        self.base_url, self.model, self.summaries = base_url, model, 0

    def _post(self, messages, tools=None):
        body = {"model": self.model, "messages": messages, "temperature": 0, **({"tools": tools} if tools else {})}
        return requests.post(f"{self.base_url}/chat/completions", json=body, timeout=120).json()

    def fit(self):
        """Summarise-to-fit: if over budget, replace old turns with one model-written summary."""
        if count_tokens(self.messages) <= self.budget:
            return
        system, old, recent = self.messages[0], self.messages[1:-self.keep_last], self.messages[-self.keep_last:]
        transcript = "\n".join(f"{m['role']}: {m['content']}" for m in old if m.get("content"))
        prompt = f"Summarise the conversation in one line.\n<transcript>\n{transcript}\n</transcript>"
        summary = self._post([{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
        self.messages = [{"role": "system", "content": f"{system['content']}\nEarlier: {summary}"}, *recent]
        self.summaries += 1

    def send(self, text, max_steps=4):
        self.messages.append({"role": "user", "content": text})
        self.fit()  # budget check BEFORE every model call
        for _ in range(max_steps):
            reply = self._post(self.messages, TOOLS)["choices"][0]["message"]
            self.messages.append(reply)
            if not reply.get("tool_calls"):
                return reply["content"]
            for call in reply["tool_calls"]:
                args = json.loads(call["function"]["arguments"])
                fn = {"save_memory": self.memory.save, "recall_memory": self.memory.recall}[call["function"]["name"]]
                self.messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call["id"], "content": fn(next(iter(args.values())))})
        return "stopped: max_steps"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    db = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "memory_demo.db"
    db.unlink(missing_ok=True)  # fresh demo each run
    chat = Chat(MemoryStore(str(db)))
    for text in ["Remember that the staging database is on port 5433.", "Thanks. Now tell me a fun fact about otters.",
                 "And one about penguins please, keep it short."]:
        print(f"> {text}\n  {chat.send(text)}\n  tokens={count_tokens(chat.messages)} summaries={chat.summaries}")
    print("system now:", chat.messages[0]["content"].splitlines()[-1])
    chat.memory.close()
    later = Chat(MemoryStore(str(db)))  # new conversation: empty history, same SQLite file
    print("> What do you remember about staging?\n ", later.send("What do you remember about staging?"))
    later.memory.close()

title: Build an MCP server and client
description: Write a stdio MCP server (JSON-RPC 2.0) and a client that discovers its era, lists tools and calls them - per MCP 2026-07-28 with a 2025-11-25 fallback.
outcome: You can expose tools over MCP without a framework, call them from your own client, and tell protocol errors from tool errors.
environment: Python 3.12 (macOS: brew python@3.12; Windows: python.org installer + py launcher) (stdlib only); MCP spec 2026-07-28 (current) + 2025-11-25 (legacy handshake); equivalent (pending-ci): official MCP Python SDK mcp 2.3.0
overview: An MCP server is a process that answers tools/list and tools/call over newline-delimited JSON-RPC; since 2026-07-28 every request carries its own protocol version.

glossary.meaning: Model Context Protocol: JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol between hosts/clients and servers that offer tools, resources and prompts.
Client launches the server as a subprocess; one JSON-RPC message per line on stdin/stdout; logs on stderr.
2026-07-28 method returning supported versions and capabilities; servers MUST implement it.
2025-11-25 (legacy) handshake; removed in 2026-07-28, still used by older servers.
Flag in a tools/call result marking a tool execution error the model can read.

concepts: Protocol version travels in _meta on every request (2026-07-28).
Probe with server/discover, fall back to initialize for legacy servers.
Protocol errors vs tool execution errors (isError).
stdout carries protocol messages only.
inRealSystems: llama.cpp's llama-server (experimental feature) can launch stdio MCP servers from a JSON config (--mcp-servers-config) and offer their tools to the model.
The official SDKs (Python mcp 2.3.0, TypeScript) implement both eras; Client(mode='auto') probes server/discover then falls back.
useWhen: When tools are shared by several agents or hosts or need their own process; a local function is simpler for one script.

title: Guardrails basics
description: Wrap an agent in deterministic checks: allow-listed tools, argument limits, injection screening of retrieved text, human approval for risky tools, secret redaction.
outcome: You can show a prompt-injection attack succeed against an unguarded agent and fail against layered checks in code.
environment: Python 3.12 (macOS: brew python@3.12; Windows: python.org installer + py launcher), requests 2.34.2; guards.py (stdlib); fake_model_server.py (obeys injected instructions on purpose); optional: Ollama 0.40.12 + qwen2.5:1.5b
overview: Assume the model can be fooled; put cheap, deterministic checks on every input, tool call, retrieved text and output so a fooled model cannot do damage.

glossary.meaning: Input that changes the model's behaviour in unintended ways; indirect when it arrives in retrieved content (OWASP LLM01:2025).
Replacing suspicious retrieved text with a placeholder before the model sees it.
A callback that must say yes before a risky tool runs; default no.
Replacing secrets in output with [REDACTED] before anyone sees it.

concepts: The model is not a security boundary.
Retrieved text is data, never instructions.
Risky tools: allow-list + approval (default no) + argument rules.
Scan outputs and tool arguments for secrets.
inRealSystems: OWASP LLM01:2025 lists least privilege, human approval for high-risk actions, segregating external content and output validation as mitigations.
MCP requires servers to validate inputs, rate-limit and sanitise outputs, and hosts to get consent before invoking tools.
llama-server warns its built-in --tools must not be enabled in untrusted environments and limits CORS to localhost when they are on.
useWhen: Always when an agent has tools with side effects, private data or untrusted input - start with allow-list + approval.
